readerTitle: Two new cleaning businesses. Only one is a startup.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (청소 서비스 두 곳, 식당의 밀키트) + 스타트업 정의에 관한 실제 저술 (Steve Blank, Paul Graham)
insight: 스타트업은 기술이나 나이가 아니라 '아직 통하는 사업 방식을 모르는 상태'다. 그래서 할 일이 실행이 아니라 탐색이다.
misconception: 새로 시작한 회사, 특히 앱이나 기술을 쓰는 회사는 모두 스타트업이다.

sources.text: Blank, S. (2010). What's A Startup? First Principles. steveblank.com
청소 서비스, 식당 밀키트 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Steve Blank의 정의 "a temporary organization designed to search for a repeatable and scalable business model"의 원문 표현과 게시 연도(2010)를 게시 전 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 인용부호 없이 풀어 썼습니다.
Paul Graham의 "Startup = Growth"(2012) 에세이에서 스타트업을 '빠르게 성장하도록 설계된 회사'로 정의한 부분을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 풀어 쓴 표현만 사용했습니다.
카드에 실패율 같은 통계는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다. 수치를 추가하려면 1차 출처를 먼저 확보하세요.

cards.title: Two new cleaning businesses. Only one is a startup.
body: Maya and Sam each start a house-cleaning business in the same town, in the same month. Same mops, same vans, same tiny budget.
A year from now, one of them will be running a business. The other will still be figuring out what the business is. That difference has a name.

image.label: Two identical cleaning vans parked side by side
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 같은 동네 길가에 똑같이 생긴 청소 서비스 밴 두 대. 한 대 옆에는 정돈된 체크리스트, 다른 한 대 옆에는 물음표가 붙은 지도. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which one is the startup?
body: **Maya** offers weekly home cleans at the usual local price and advertises in neighborhood groups. Thousands of businesses already work this way.
**Sam** cleans short-term rental homes between guests, priced per turnover and booked automatically from hosts' calendars. Nobody nearby does it, and he doesn't yet know if hosts will pay.

options.text: Maya. She's new, and she uses a booking app
options.feedback: Being new and using an app feels startup-like. But her model is already proven elsewhere, so her risk is doing it well, not finding out what works.

options.text: Sam. He still doesn't know if his model works
options.feedback: Yes. Sam has to discover who pays, how much, and how to find them again. That open question is what makes his business a startup.

options.text: Both. Any new business is a startup
options.feedback: Both are new, and both carry risk. But treating them the same hides that they need to spend their first year doing very different work.

cards.title: Maya executes. Sam searches.
body: Maya's questions have known answers. How do I hire good cleaners? How do I keep quality steady? Other owners can tell her.
Sam's questions have no answers yet. Will hosts pay $40 a turnover, or only $25? Do they find him through rental groups or property managers? Will they stay after the first month?
Nobody can tell him. He has to **find out**, cheaply, before he runs out of money.

image.label: Left: a clear checklist. Right: a map with question marks
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Execute": 체크 표시가 된 할 일 목록. 오른쪽 "Search": 여러 갈래 길에 물음표가 붙은 지도와 작은 손전등.

cards.title: A startup is a search
body: A **startup** is a business that is still searching for a way of making money that works, can be repeated, and can grow.

Entrepreneur and teacher Steve Blank put it roughly this way in 2010: a startup is a temporary organization built to search for a repeatable, scalable business model. Writer and investor Paul Graham adds a second test: a startup is designed to grow fast.
Neither definition mentions technology, age or size.

cards.title: The questions a startup must answer
body: A search ends when you can answer these with evidence, not hope:
list: **What** will they pay for, and how much?
**How** do you reach them again and again?
**Can it grow** without costs growing just as fast?
cards.callout: When the answers are proven, the startup has become a company. The job shifts from searching to executing.
cards.softwareNote: A new app that copies a proven tool for a known market is closer to Maya than to Sam. A small software team selling something nobody has paid for yet is searching, even if the code is easy.

cards.title: A stage, not a label
body: Startup describes a moment, not a type of company. If Sam's turnover model works, he becomes a business like Maya's, just a newer kind.
It also works the other way. A 30-year-old company that launches something truly new is running a startup inside itself. A brand-new franchise that follows a tested playbook is not.
So the useful question isn't "are we a startup?" It's "which parts of our business are still unknown?"

image.label: A timeline from 'search' to 'execute'
image.brief: 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 가는 길. 왼쪽 구간은 안개와 물음표("Searching"), 가운데 "Model proven" 깃발, 오른쪽 구간은 곧은 고속도로("Executing"). 작은 청소 밴이 깃발을 지나는 장면.

cards.title: A startup isn't a better business.
body: Searching is expensive and uncertain. Many searches end without finding a model that works. Maya's proven path may give her a steadier income much sooner.

The common mistake is mixing up the two modes. Searchers who act as if they already know the answers hire, lease and advertise too early. Owners of proven models who keep "searching" never settle into doing the work well.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: Your family restaurant has been profitable for eight years. Regulars keep asking for take-home meal kits of your best dishes. You've never sold kits, and you don't know what they'd cost to make, ship or keep fresh.
How do you start?

options.text: Lease a second kitchen and hire staff. The restaurant proves people love the food
options.feedback: The restaurant proves the recipes, not the kit business. You'd be paying execution costs before answering search questions like price, reorders and spoilage.

options.text: Sell 30 kits a week from your current kitchen and track who reorders
options.feedback: You treat the kits as a small startup inside a proven business. You learn the unknowns cheaply, then invest once the answers are real.

options.text: Skip it. The restaurant works, so why risk anything
options.feedback: This protects a business you know works. But you give up a cheap chance to learn whether customers' requests turn into paid orders.

cards.title: A startup is a business that is still searching for a model that works.
body: Know whether you're searching or executing, and spend your money to match.
**Try it today:** write down the four questions from this lesson. For your business, or a new idea, mark each one *proven* or *still a guess*.
